name: Jalebi
description: Crisp Pakistani jalebi spirals made from a lightly fermented flour batter, fried at controlled heat and dipped briefly in warm cardamom syrup.
ingredients: About 3/4 cup lukewarm water, added gradually
Neutral oil or ghee for frying
method: Mix the plain flour, cornflour and yeast. Whisk in the lukewarm water gradually until the batter is thick but pipeable, then cover and leave in a warm place until lightly bubbly rather than dramatically risen.

For the syrup, simmer the sugar, water and crushed cardamom until the sugar dissolves and the syrup lightly coats a spoon. Stir in the lemon juice and keep it warm and fluid without reducing it into a heavy syrup.
Transfer the batter to a squeeze bottle or piping bag with a small opening. Heat the frying oil over medium heat and test with a little batter; it should rise steadily without darkening immediately.
Pipe compact connected spirals directly into the oil, working in small batches. Fry gently and turn as needed until both sides are evenly golden and crisp.
Move the hot jalebi into the warm syrup for only a short soak, turning so both sides are coated. Leaving crisp jalebi in syrup too long can soften the surface.
Lift out, allow excess syrup to drain and serve warm while the spirals still have a crisp bite.
tips: Let the batter become lightly bubbly before frying; if it spreads too much, whisk in a small spoonful of flour.
Keep the syrup warm and fluid. Thick, cool syrup coats unevenly and can make the jalebi heavy.
Pipe compact spirals and fry in small batches so you can control the colour.
storage: Jalebi has its best texture when freshly made. If leftovers are stored, keep them covered and restore some crispness with gentle dry heat before serving rather than soaking them again.
serving: Serve warm on its own or alongside a cup of unsweetened chai.
image_alt: Pakistani jalebi spirals fried crisp and coated with glossy cardamom sugar syrup
image_caption: Crisp jalebi spirals with a light fermented batter and a thin glossy coating of warm cardamom syrup.
technique: Jalebi depends on two consistencies: batter that flows in a controlled ribbon and syrup that coats without setting hard. Fry at moderate heat until the spirals are crisp, then dip briefly while jalebi and syrup are compatible in temperature.
doneness_cues: Rested batter should flow in a continuous ribbon that can hold a spiral instead of spreading flat in the oil.
Oil should bubble steadily around the batter without browning the jalebi immediately.
Fried jalebi should feel crisp at the edges before it enters the syrup.
Syrup should cling in a glossy layer; a heavy crystallised coating means it has become too concentrated.
mistakes: Using very thin batter, which spreads and cannot hold the spiral shape.
Frying too hot, which darkens the outside before enough moisture leaves the centre.
Leaving crisp jalebi in syrup too long, which softens it.
Overcooking syrup or stirring crystallising sugar around the sides of the pan.
substitutions: A piping bottle, squeeze bottle or strong piping bag can be used; choose an opening that gives a controllable medium-thin stream.
Cardamom can be kept subtle so it supports rather than dominates the fermented aroma.
If the rested batter thickens too much, adjust with water a teaspoon at a time rather than making a large correction.
reheating: Jalebi is best fresh. If it softens, brief dry heat can restore some crispness, but reheating syrup-coated jalebi too aggressively can make the sugar sticky or burn.

faqs.question: Why is my jalebi not crispy?
faqs.answer: The batter may be too thin, the oil may be too cool, the jalebi may be under-fried, or it may have remained in syrup too long.

faqs.question: Why does jalebi batter spread in the oil?
faqs.answer: It is usually too thin or not rested enough to develop body. Adjust with a small amount of flour and test one spiral.

faqs.question: How long should jalebi stay in syrup?
faqs.answer: Only long enough to take on a light coating while keeping its structure. A long soak makes crisp jalebi soft.
